drills.coachNote: That rook on d1 has been hanging on the file this whole time, with your queen on d3 staring straight at it and only the e1 rook backing it up. Qxa3 grabs a stray pawn but abandons that idea completely, and it also leaves your f5 pawn loose to White's queen on h5 — after Qxf5, Qxb4, Rc1, and Qf4, White claws back over two pawns of the huge lead you had. Qxd1 takes the bigger prize right away; even though White answers Qxf7+ Kxf7 Rxd1 to win the queen back, you've traded a bishop for a full rook and stay comfortably on top. When your queen already threatens a rook, don't settle for a pawn instead.

drills.coachNote: White's king has just one defender on f2, and you already had two attackers pointed at it — the bishop on h4 and the queen on c2. Bf6 is a safe retreat, but it lets that chance slip; White gets to play Ng5, and after Bxg5 Qxg5 f4 White stirs up real trouble near your king, costing you roughly 1.6 pawns of your edge. Bxf2+ cashes in immediately: the king can't recapture because your queen covers f2 along the rank, so Kh1 is forced, and after Bf7, Qg5, Bxe1, Rxe1 you come out with extra material and the initiative intact. When two of your pieces already gang up on one weak square by the enemy king, take it before it goes away.

drills.coachNote: White wants that knight hop to f5, burrowing into your position and stirring up trouble around your kingside pawns while you're not doing anything active yourself. Qb6 sidesteps but doesn't stop it — after Nf5, Rd7, Qc3, Qg6 you're forced onto the back foot defending, and nearly four pawns of your equal position slip away. Qe3 instead creates your own problem for White first: it eyes the d3 pawn and the diagonal straight down to the king on b1, so after Qe3 Qxc7 Qxd3+ Ka1 Rd7 Qe5 you're the one giving checks while White's queen is stuck on the wrong side of the board. With an exposed king, look for the move that threatens something, not the one that just retreats.
drills.threat: White's knight on g3 is ready to jump to f5, digging into your kingside while your queen on c5 sits idle.

drills.coachNote: Right now your bishop on d3 is held up by just one piece, the queen on d1 sitting behind it on the file, and Black's bishop on g6 is already lined up on that exact diagonal. Qb3 walks the queen off the file to snatch at the knight on b4, but that strips d3's only guard; Black plays Bxd3, and after Nxa7 Kxa7 Qxb4 you've swapped your bishop for a single pawn — about 4.3 pawns of eval gone in four moves. Rc7 keeps the pressure without that cost: it invades the seventh rank, and after Qxc7 Nxc7 Bxd3 Re1 Kxc7 you trade queens favorably and still come out ahead materially. Before moving the piece that's guarding something, check what you're about to leave hanging.
drills.threat: Your bishop on d3 has exactly one defender — the queen on d1 — and Black's bishop on g6 already eyes that same diagonal.

drills.coachNote: Black's king is still sitting on c8, and a7 is an open fork square — a knight landing there with check would hit the king and grab material besides. Bh2 tucks your bishop out of the way, but it lets Black play Bxh2+ Kxh2, an even trade that costs you nothing materially yet hands over the tempo for Kb8, which shuts that fork down for good — your crushing +4.6 edge drops by 3.6 pawns for no real return. Nb5 cashes the fork in right now: after Bxf4 Nxa7+ Kc7 exf4 Bxd3 you grab the a7 pawn with check, recapture on f4, and end up with even more material while Black's king is still stuck in the middle. When the enemy king hasn't castled and a fork square is open, take it before it disappears.

drills.coachNote: Your king is safe and White's king on g1 is trapped by its own pawns on g3 and h3, plus your rook already sitting on f2 cutting off the second rank. That means your queen just needs one more square to deliver mate, and Qg2 is it — g1 has no flight square, nothing blocks it, nothing can capture it. Instead you played Rxb2, grabbing a pawn instead of mating, which let White claw back with Nd2 and Qc2 instead of the game just ending, turning a forced mate into merely a big advantage. Kf3 gets you to the useful square directly, so after Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 Kf7 you've made the identical progress a move faster.
